 FILE PHOTO — Voters arriving at Bridgeport City Hall on Election Day, Nov. 5, 2024. Credit: Johnathon Henninger / CTNewsJunkie 
 Tuesday’s debate between Gov. Ned Lamont and challenger Ryan Fazio played out essentially like last week’s, albeit with different hosts and questions.
 Lamont, the two-term Democratic incumbent, pointed to his record and brought up President Donald Trump and his policies several times. Fazio, the Republican state senator from Greenwich, touted his plans, and criticized Lamont for the state’s tax rate and affordability.
 “When he first ran for office, Governor Lamont promised, I will cut your property taxes. Those are his words, not anyone else’s,” Fazio said. “Over the last eight years that he’s been in office, because of his policies, property taxes have gone up by 30% or more in most of our municipalities. That’s a broken promise and it’s unaffordability that Connecticut cannot take any longer.”
 Lamont in his opening, reiterated his claim that he was the only governor to have cut the income tax since its inception in 1991. He said in his previous campaigns he had run against a Republican who had promised to eliminate the income tax.
 “I think you’ve heard that for about 30 years,” he said. “We’re the ones that have stepped forward, kept our promise and cut the income tax.”
 Joe DeLong, executive director of the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities, who served as a panelist alongside moderators Dennis House and Kathryn Hauser of WTNH News, wanted to know how Lamont planned to address the strain that special education placed on local school budgets and by extension, local property taxes.
 “Should the state commit to paying a larger guaranteed share, even if that leaves less money for other state priorities?” he asked.
 Lamont acknowledged that the state was having a hard time keeping up with the need for funding, even with consistent budget increases.
 “Autism and other needs are growing fast and could be 30% of (school) budgets right now,” he said.
 While saying he wanted the state to take more of the lead on special education, he disagreed with the premise of DeLong’s question.
 “I do not want more money just for the status quo,” he said. “I want to see how the state can make a real difference: make it easier for you to take care of these kids locally; have us negotiate with all the private providers so we can get a better for folks. And put in place an insurance pool so if your small town ends up with two or three kids you didn’t expect with real needs, we can make a difference. We’re going to do more, but just not more of the same.”
 DeLong directed a question about Fazio’s property tax cap proposal to the challenger.
 “If a city or town’s school and special education costs rise faster, who covers the difference?” he asked.
 Fazio in response, said he agreed with everything Lamont had said about special education costs.
 “The problem is he’s had eight years to accomplish it and he hasn’t. The buck has to stop somewhere,” he said.
 Fazio said his proposal hinged on the state rescinding what he called hundreds of unfunded mandates on towns, which he said was responsible for driving up property taxes. While not specifying any mandates that should be repealed, he said it could be done with proper leadership.
 Hauser asked about home heating oil prices, noting that projections were as high as 50% above last year – an estimated $2,800 average for the winter.
 “What plan do you have to help families that don’t qualify for low-income assistance but have trouble paying their bills this year?” she asked.
 Lamont immediately criticized Trump and the war in Iran as being the primary driver behind the price increases. He noted that the state’s relief fund had passed with bipartisan support in the state House of Representatives, pointedly mentioning that Senate Republicans had been less supportive.
 “That’s allowed us to say, ‘Look, we’re going to provide additional support for those people so they don’t go cold this winter,’” he said. “But these are the type of price increases that are coming to us from Washington, D.C.”
 The debate, held at Mohegan Sun, featured a mostly quiet audience. Lamont drew one of the rare chuckles and applause in response to a question originally directed at Fazio regarding independence from the Trump administration.
 After stating that traditional New England Republicans would be outraged by the current administration’s actions, Lamont noted that he had been challenged to a primary by Hamden progressive state Rep. Josh Elliott.
 “A guy ran against me saying Lamont refuses to raise taxes. Now I’m running against a guy saying, ‘Lamont, all he does is raise taxes,’” he said. “Maybe these two guys should have a debate and then come in and tell me what they decide. I do what I think is right every day.”
 In a lightning round, both candidates said they had not used AI to prepare for the debate.
 Asked what town they would live in beside Greenwich (both candidates’ hometown) or Hartford, Fazio hedged and said the north-central region, before settling on Suffield or a similar overlooked community. Lamont pointed to a handful of mayors in the audience before saying Stonington was “pretty cool.”
 Lamont struggled to answer a question about misconceptions involving politicians, prompting Fazio to respond that “clearly a misconception is that they’re decisive.”
 Fazio, who has made his resemblance to Clark Kent part of his political messaging, drew a laugh from the audience and Lamont responding to a question about the best Halloween costume he had ever worn.
 “It’s so silly to say, probably Clark Kent” he said.
 Lamont, who frequently wears a Grateful Dead belt at political functions, said he had not yet worn his favorite costume.
 “This Saturday, I’ll be Jerry Garcia,” he said.
 On a somewhat-related question asked next, both candidates said they had never made a purchase from a state cannabis shop.
 In closing, both candidates returned to their campaign talking points. Fazio said the campaign was about affordability and taxes.
 “Now, it’s time for a change,” he said.
 Lamont touted the difference between now and eight years ago, noting that the 2017 state budget was delivered months late and disputing that Connecticut had become a less desirable place to live. He revisited an earlier question about housing, saying the reason it was needed is because more people want to live in Connecticut.
